questions.q: What is the first section of the CTA-style presentation structure this lesson describes?
options: The design diagram and narrative
Risks and mitigations
A list of every Apex class name used in the implementation
Business context and requirements, stated explicitly before any technical content
questions.explain: The structure starts with business context and requirements stated up front, before technical content, so the reviewer has the actual need in view before evaluating the design against it.

questions.q: What does 'requirements traceability' mean in the context of presenting a design to a review board?
options: Being able to trace every significant design decision back to a specific, previously-stated requirement or constraint, rather than leaving the connection implicit
Listing every field mapping used in the integration
Tracking how long each Apex class takes to execute
Ensuring every requirement is written in formal UML notation
questions.explain: Traceability means the reviewer doesn't have to guess why a decision was made -- each decision explicitly connects back to a stated need, like Doverfield's event-driven ERP sync tracing back to its delay-tolerance and non-blocking requirements.

questions.q: What should a review-ready integration diagram include, and what should it leave out, per this lesson?
options: It should include every field mapping and every Apex class name for completeness
It should only show the business requirements, with no technical content at all
It should show system boundaries, data flow direction, and specific integration points, while leaving out field-mapping and class-level detail that belongs in supporting documentation instead
It should be a single unlabeled box representing the entire Salesforce org
questions.explain: A diagram cluttered with implementation-level detail buries the structural information (boundaries, flow, integration points) the diagram exists to communicate -- that detail belongs in supporting documentation instead.

questions.q: Why does presenting only the final chosen pattern, with no alternatives mentioned, read poorly to a review board?
options: Because review boards require at least three diagrams per presentation
Because it reads as either lucky or untested -- stating the alternatives considered and the specific reason each was rejected is what demonstrates the choice was actually deliberate
Because Salesforce requires every design to include a written alternatives section by policy
Because a single pattern can never be the correct final answer
questions.explain: Lesson 15's comparison-matrix reasoning is exactly what turns a bare final choice into a demonstrated, deliberate tradeoff -- naming the rejected alternatives and why they lost is what makes the choice legible as reasoned rather than accidental.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say assumptions should be stated up front in the presentation, rather than only when challenged?
options: Because assumptions are not actually part of architecture work
Because review boards never ask questions about assumptions
Because stating assumptions up front removes the need for a risks-and-mitigations section
Because an assumption surfaced only when challenged looks like it was never actually considered, even if it was
questions.explain: Proactively naming assumptions demonstrates they were deliberately considered as part of the design process, rather than appearing to be an afterthought only produced under direct questioning.
